outcome: The existence question for the degree-57 Moore graph remains completely open, but two post-window results narrowed the space of possible constructions/automorphisms: Smith & Montemanni (2024, 2026) ruled out larger classes of symmetric candidate constructions via computer search, and Ishida (2026) proved any such graph's automorphism group must have odd order (no involutions).

ai.basis_quote: The derivation given here uses neither the computer search nor the tabulated bounds [of previous analyses].

summary: This is the classic 'missing Moore graph' problem: does a Moore graph of diameter 2, girth 5, degree 57 (order 3250) exist? It has been open for over six decades and remains open today. Three lines of post-window work narrow the search without resolving it. (1) Smith & Montemanni, 'Potential Subgraphs of the Missing Moore Graph' (Symmetry, published online 2024-11-22), used Google OR-Tools' CP-SAT constraint solver — a classical constraint/SAT solver, not an AI system under these codes — to extend the known potential t-subgraphs (candidate local structures) from 15 to 20, assuming a cyclic group of permutations on the tree branches; this is a computational search extension, not a resolution of any case. (2) The same authors' follow-up, 'The Moore Graph of Diameter 2 and Degree 57 via Cyclic Derangements' (Axioms, submitted 2026-02-06, published 2026-05-01), proves that a construction of the graph using only a cyclic group of derangement permutations is impossible, closing off that entire restricted family of candidate constructions (a case/sub-family ruled out, hence partial progress, though the paper frames it as narrowing rather than settling anything about the general existence question — no counterexample or resolution results, so this is 'progress' rather than 'partial': the paper shows no such graph exists *of this restricted symmetric type*, which is arguably a partial resolution of a special-case non-existence, but since the general problem (as literally stated in the bullet, with no symmetry assumption) is untouched and the special case was itself invented by these researchers rather than being a natural 'restriction of the stated question' with independent interest, I read it as scope-narrowing progress; see competing_reading). No AI system is mentioned in either Smith/Montemanni paper. (3) Ishida, 'No involutions in the missing Moore graph' (arXiv 2606.29183, submitted 2026-06-28, revised 2026-07-08) proves algebraically (via a trace-rank identity from Brauer quotients of p-permutation lattices) that if the degree-57 Moore graph exists, its automorphism group has odd order — ruling out involutions. This is a genuine new structural constraint on any hypothetical solution, i.e. progress, not a case-restriction of the stated existence question itself (an automorphism-group constraint is a property any hypothetical graph would have to satisfy, not a restriction of the parameters in the question), so it is best classified as `progress` rather than `partial`. The author's affiliation is listed as 'A.I. System Research, Inc., Kyoto, Japan' — a company name containing 'A.I.' — but the paper itself explicitly disclaims computer or AI assistance: 'The derivation given here uses neither the computer search nor the tabulated bounds' of prior analyses. This is a pure algebraic/representation-theoretic proof; ai_role is `none`. Notably, a different 2026-06 preprint from the same research organization (Ryosuke Mizuno, 'A.I. System Research Co., Ltd.'), 'New lower bounds for the degree/diameter problem via interaction with a browser-accessible LLM' (arXiv 2606.15860), does describe substantial ChatGPT (gpt-5-5-pro) involvement in discovering new graph constructions — but that paper addresses different degree/diameter parameters (N(12,5) and N(16,5)), not the degree-57 girth-5 Moore graph, so it is a related-but-distinct problem under §3.1 and not counted here. I also checked Epoch AI's FrontierMath 'Open Problems' page, which lists the missing Moore graph explicitly as an AI benchmark target problem, but states no AI system has made any progress on it. Overall: real, human-driven mathematical progress narrowing the space of possible constructions and automorphism groups, but the core existence question is untouched, and no AI system is credited with any of it.
competing_reading: The Smith & Montemanni 'Cyclic Derangements' non-existence result for the cyclic-group-only construction could instead be read as `partial` if one treats 'Moore graph of degree 57 constructible via a cyclic group of derangements' as a genuine case/sub-instance of the stated existence question (a restriction on the automorphism group, akin to restricting a variable). Under that reading, the correct classification would be `partial` with `resolution_direction: refuted` for that sub-case, since a class of constructions was proven impossible. I chose `progress` because the cyclic-derangement construction method is itself a technique invented by these researchers to search for the graph, not a natural sub-family carved out of the problem's own stated parameters (degree, girth, order), so ruling it out narrows the search space without settling any piece of the actual mathematical object described in the bullet. A careful reader could reasonably disagree and call it `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A full computational or algebraic proof (or explicit construction) resolving the existence question outright, or a case-restriction on the problem's own stated parameters (degree 57, girth 5) — as opposed to a restriction on the search method — being settled.

judgement.doubts: Structural constraints on a hypothetical graph (automorphism group, construction method) are treated as narrowing, in the tradition of Higman/Mačaj–Širáň, not as settling a case of the existence question; the cyclic-derangement result could be read as a refuted sub-case (partial), as the record's competing_reading notes, but the restriction is on a search technique, not on the bullet's parameters. The MDPI texts were not read directly. Ishida's affiliation name contains 'A.I.' but the paper claims no AI involvement; the LLM paper by Mizuno concerns different parameters.
